::: {.at-a-glance}
- **Time:** 80 minutes in class (swap and reproduce), then at home (release and Zenodo, 30 minutes).
- **Slides:** [Putting it all together](../lectures/12-putting-it-together/12-putting-it-together.qmd)
- **You need:** your `ltee-project` and your capstone project on GitHub with green *Reproduce* checks; a partner.
- **You will have:** a reproduce report on your partner's project (and one on yours), a released version of your project with a Zenodo DOI, and a checklist.
:::

## Overview

All these tools, one question: **can someone else get your results, from
your repository alone, without asking you?** Today you find out, with a
classmate as the "someone else". Then you freeze a version of your project,
give it a permanent identifier (a DOI) and archive it, so the answer stays yes
after GitHub, the course and maybe you have moved on.

The five pillars of computational reproducibility (Ziemann et al. 2023), and
where this course covered them:

| Pillar | Lessons |
|--------|---------|
| Literate programming | [06 Jupyter](06-jupyter.qmd), [07 Quarto](07-quarto.qmd) |
| Code version control and sharing | [04 Git](04-git.qmd), this lesson |
| Compute environment control | [05 Pixi](05-pixi.qmd), [08 Containers](08-containers.qmd) |
| Persistent data sharing | [03 Data management](03-data-management.qmd), this lesson |
| Documentation | [11 Documentation](11-documentation.qmd), [02 Project organization](02-project-organization.qmd) |

and the glue between them: workflows ([09](09-snakemake.qmd),
[10](10-nextflow.qmd)) and automatic checks (the *Reproduce* GitHub Action).

### Learning outcomes

After this lesson you can:

1. **Reproduce** someone else's project from a clean clone using only its documentation, and **report** what worked and what did not.
2. **Release** a version of your project and **archive** it on Zenodo with a DOI.
3. **Apply** a checklist of reproducible practices at each phase of a new project.

Checks: the reproduce report you file (outcome 1); the DOI badge in your
README (outcome 2); your capstone, graded with the
[capstone rubric](../assessment/capstone-rubric.qmd) (all).

## 1. Before the swap: is your own project ready?

Check the three things your partner will hit first, in a clean state:

```{.bash .run}
cd ~/cbio7501/ltee-project
pixi install --locked
pixi exec cffconvert --validate -i CITATION.cff
pixi run reproduce
```

```{.bash .run-ci}
git status --short
```

`git status` must show nothing important uncommitted: anything that is only on
your laptop will be missing for your partner. Push, and check that the
*Reproduce* check on GitHub is green.

## 2. Swap and reproduce (60 minutes)

Pair up. Each of you reproduces the other's capstone project (and, if time
allows, their `ltee-project`). Rules:

- Use **only the repository**: the README and what it links to. Do not ask
  your partner, do not look over their shoulder.
- Start from a **clean clone** in a new folder.
- Write a **reproduce report** as you go: copy the
  [template](../assessment/reproduce-report-template.qmd) into a new issue on
  your partner's repository and fill it in.

```{.bash .norun}
cd ~/cbio7501
git clone git@github.com:PARTNER/PROJECT.git partner-project
cd partner-project
pixi run reproduce        # or whatever the README says
```

Things to record: how long it took, every command you had to guess, every
error message (in full), and whether your numbers match theirs. For the LTEE
project, `pixi run compare-workflows` and the variant counts in the README give
you an exact comparison.

::: {.callout-note title="Discuss with your partner afterwards (15 minutes)"}
Read each other's reports together. Which problem would have stopped a
stranger? Which one fix would help most? Fix it before you hand
in the capstone.
:::

## 3. Release and archive on Zenodo

A Git commit can be rewritten and a GitHub repository can be deleted. A
**release** on Zenodo is a permanent, citable copy of one version, with a
**DOI**. Zenodo (run by CERN) keeps it, and every new release gets its own DOI
under one "concept" DOI that always points to the latest version (the Scotland
wastewater record in [lesson 03](03-data-management.qmd) is an example).

Practise first on the **Zenodo sandbox** (<https://sandbox.zenodo.org/>), a
copy of Zenodo for testing whose DOIs are not real. When you are sure, repeat
on <https://zenodo.org/>.

1. **Log in to Zenodo with your GitHub account** (or ORCID, and link GitHub
   under your account settings).
2. **Enable the repository.** In Zenodo, open the *GitHub* page from your
   profile menu, press *Sync*, and switch on your repository. From now on,
   Zenodo archives every GitHub release of it.
3. **Check the metadata.** Zenodo uses your `CITATION.cff` for the title,
   authors, ORCID iDs and license (unless the repository also has a
   `.zenodo.json`, which then takes over). Make sure it is valid
   ([lesson 11](11-documentation.qmd)).
4. **Tag and release.** On your laptop, tag the commit you hand in, push the
   tag, then on GitHub choose *Releases → Draft a new release*, pick the tag,
   write what this version contains, and *Publish release*:

```{.bash .run-ci}
git switch main
git pull
git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "Version handed in for CBIO7501"
git push origin v1.0.0
```

5. **Get the DOI.** After a minute, the release appears in Zenodo with a DOI
   and a DOI badge. Add the badge to the top of your README, and the DOI to
   `CITATION.cff` (`doi: 10.5281/zenodo.NNNNNNN`), then commit and push.

### What else to archive

A code release is not the whole analysis. For a publication, also deposit,
and link from the README:

- **the data**, if it is not already in a repository (here it is: figshare, NCBI);
- **the container image** saved with `docker save` ([lesson 08](08-containers.qmd#archive-and-share-the-image)),
  as a file in the same Zenodo record or a linked one;
- **the rendered report** (`reports/ltee-report.html`) as supplementary material.

## Break it: the file that was only on your laptop

The most common reason a swap fails: something the analysis needs was never
committed. See it happen. Add a helper the report would use, but do not commit
it, then clone the project the way your partner does:

```{.bash .run-ci}
cd ~/cbio7501/ltee-project
printf 'MIN_GENERATION = 5000\n' > scripts/settings.py
git status --short scripts/
cd ~/cbio7501
rm -rf ltee-clone
git clone git@github.com:ada-lovelace/ltee-project.git ltee-clone
```

```{.bash .run-ci .expect-fail}
ls ltee-clone/scripts/settings.py
```

On your laptop the file exists, so everything works for you; in the clone it
does not exist, and any code importing it fails. `git status` showed it as
untracked (`??`), and the *Reproduce* GitHub Action would have failed on the
next push: that is exactly what it is for. Clean up:

```{.bash .run-ci}
rm -rf ~/cbio7501/ltee-clone ~/cbio7501/ltee-project/scripts/settings.py
```

## 4. A checklist for your next project

Updated from the checklist in the course's opening lecture
([source](credits.qmd#week1)), with the tools from these lessons.

**Before you start**

- [ ] One folder (and one Git repository) per project, from a template ([02](02-project-organization.qmd))
- [ ] A data management plan: sources, formats, storage, licenses, sensitive data ([03](03-data-management.qmd))
- [ ] `pixi init` (or the template) with the platforms you and your collaborators use ([05](05-pixi.qmd))

**During the project**

- [ ] Raw data downloaded by a script, checksummed, read-only ([03](03-data-management.qmd))
- [ ] Small, frequent commits with clear messages; branches and pull requests ([04](04-git.qmd))
- [ ] Every tool added with `pixi add`; `pixi.toml` and `pixi.lock` committed together ([05](05-pixi.qmd))
- [ ] Steps as Pixi tasks or a workflow (Snakemake, Nextflow); settings in a config file ([09](09-snakemake.qmd))
- [ ] Results and figures made by code in a report, never pasted ([07](07-quarto.qmd))
- [ ] Decisions logged in `docs/decisions.md`
- [ ] A *Reproduce* check in CI from the first push

**At submission**

- [ ] README answers the seven questions; `CITATION.cff` valid; licenses chosen ([11](11-documentation.qmd))
- [ ] A colleague reproduced it from a clean clone (section 2)
- [ ] Data in a repository with an identifier; code released with a DOI; container image archived (section 3)
- [ ] A data and code availability statement that names all of them ([03](03-data-management.qmd))

**After publication**

- [ ] Issues answered; corrections released as new versions (new DOI, same concept DOI)
- [ ] `pixi.lock` kept; the image archived, so the old version can still be rebuilt

## 5. The capstone

Your capstone is your own mini-analysis, built with the same practices as the
LTEE project, step by step since lesson 02. It is assessed with the
[capstone rubric](../assessment/capstone-rubric.qmd), which is tied to checks
you can run yourself: the *Reproduce* GitHub Action on a clean clone, the
reproduce report from your partner, and the files above. Fix what your
partner's report found, then release the version you hand in.

## Troubleshooting

| Problem | What to do |
|---------|------------|
| Your partner's `pixi install --locked` fails | They changed `pixi.toml` without committing the new `pixi.lock`. Report it; they run `pixi install` and commit the lock file. |
| The download fails for your partner but not for you | The data was already on your laptop. Check that the download script is committed and the source URLs work. |
| Zenodo does not show your repository | Press *Sync* on the Zenodo GitHub page, and check you logged in with the right GitHub account. |
| No new Zenodo record after a release | Only releases made **after** enabling the repository are archived. Make a new release (for example `v1.0.1`). |
| The Zenodo record has the wrong authors or license | Fix `CITATION.cff` (or `.zenodo.json`) and make a new release; the old version stays as it was. |

## Apply it to your own mini-analysis

This whole lesson is about your mini-analysis: get it reproduced by your
partner, fix what they found, release it with a DOI, and hand it in.

## Key points

- The real test of reproducibility is someone else, a clean clone and only your documentation.
- Uncommitted files, guessed commands and stale lock files are the usual failures; CI catches most of them early.
- A release on Zenodo gives a version a permanent DOI; archive the data, the image and the report with it.
- Reproducibility is a habit at every phase of a project, not a step at the end.
